rationale: A spoken-query phone-style information system that interprets what the caller says matches machine recognition of speech to act on it, but the quote shows only a prompt and not 1984-style command recognition.
A vertical file called a robot memory bank points toward machine storage of records, but nothing about query matching or speed appears.
One master intelligence tuned by wavelength to every robot is central coordination of many robots, though radio-wave world domination differs from a warehouse fleet manager.
Touching a wire to record thoughts is a crude pointer to reading minds, but nothing about decoding images from brain signals.
A flickering volumetric 3D form filling the cabin matches a three-dimensional image of a person, but a projected free-floating figure differs from a cylinder multiplex hologram.
A brain of neuron-like construction that computes matches a network of neuron-like units, but the quote says nothing of learning or pattern recognition like digit reading.
A rat's leg movements via levers drive a robot body, which is animal motor signals rather than brain signals read by an implant.
Pulling up a person's master file by 'cybbing' is quick record retrieval from a stored collection, but the quote has no query-matching detail.
A chart of red and green light points showing positions of nearby ships is a live plot of tracked objects like SAGE consoles, though the detection method is fantasy.
A citizen's number fed to a master board for recording is tracking by number, only loosely related to a punched card opening dining halls.
The quote is about someone talking to a man named Snookums and shows no machine transcribing speech.
A 'business neurological instrument' hints at a device tied to the nervous system but says nothing of restoring a sense like a cochlear implant.
An implanted device triggered by a nerve-tract change sends a signal to a transceiver, matching neural signals driving a machine; the teleport use and single trigger differ from cursor control.
The quote only names a ship carrying 'the Brains' and describes no display tank or visualization.
Little machine creatures being developed as parts of a supercomputer points loosely toward a central machine with subordinate robots.
Egg-shaped treaded robots with arms rolling in show no sign of responding to speech.
A robot writing mysteries and textbooks is machine-authored text, but weather forecasts from data templates are a far narrower thing.
A machine combining EEG and computer that amplifies imagination into a world is immersive computer-fed experience, though brain-driven rather than headset displays.
A planet's surface appearing in 3D on a screen loosely resembles 3D display, but a screen is not a holographic multiplex image.
A computer built into the ship as an intrinsic part loosely suggests shipboard computing, but navigation or burns are not described.
Coloured light points moving as caravans on a game floor loosely suggest a 3D light display, with no holographic detail.
Walls of electronic file controls evoke large automated record stores, but nothing about searching them by query.
Neuro-graphs that screen entrants are a physical detection device and have nothing to do with intruding into computers.
Controlling a robot body's speed by thought is thought-driven machine control, though the quote has a whole brain in the body rather than a recorded signal moving a cursor.
A registration robot that handles cards and flags irregular ones to a manager is a machine checking an identity card, though not for access.
Ship-dots swarming across a space chart are live positions of many tracked objects like radar tracks on SAGE consoles.
Working by sheer will without hands is a tentative speculation of thought-controlled machines, with no mechanism given.
Someone picking brains while victims were dazed points toward extracting mental content, loosely.
A giant tank showing every enemy unit in exact detail is a three-dimensional tactical display, though not a hologram with a mechanism.
A wall-sized three-dimensional contour map fed from regional computers is a large 3D map display, though it is not a hologram.
Speaking a question into the Predictinformer's mouthpiece is voice input to a computer, but the quote does not show recognition of command words.
Putting a captive under Scanners hints at examining a mind, but nothing about reading specific thoughts or images.
A control panel wired to a power plant loosely resembles a prosthetic person controlling machines, but not an implant restoring a sense.
Mandatory shipboard computers planning courses match computers steering a ship, but the quote has no orbital maneuvering detail.
A pilot computer holding automatic course projection corresponds to a computer calculating spacecraft courses, though not tied to a burn.
Instruments that are themselves robots hint at machine-made music, but this is hardware that plays rather than computer-played notes.
Robot teachers drawing on one central Brain loosely echo a central computer directing many robots, but not a warehouse fleet.
The claim that the exchange might be telepathy points to direct mind-machine contact, but the quote gives no mechanism.
A robot speaking through a small speaker to grant guest status is synthesized voice output, but nothing about how the voice is generated.
An electronic device that teaches a student matches a machine presenting lessons, but no testing or grading appears.
Speaking into a mike to speed up robot crews is voice-commanded machines, but recognition is not described.
A remote-controlled double of a specific man matches a robot made as a copy of a particular person, though no human likeness comes from a real 1964 figure.
A photoelectric tracer with a coded description for an unlimited file search matches machine search of stored records, though by image.
Communicators keyed into census files with running totals are networked terminals loosely, but SAGE links radar sites, which differs.
Tape-reading electronic eyes selecting words to send is loosely optical reading, but the output is speech rather than character recognition.
Robots controlled by voice, not radio, match machines carrying out spoken commands, but recognition detail is absent.
A house that runs itself matches an automated home, though the quote offers no sensing or occupant response.
Computers computing orbits and trajectories for scout ships match computed orbital maneuvers, but they are ground-based and not described as onboard.
A ship brain comparing candidate worlds with its stored database is loosely retrieval, but its function is judgment more than query matching.
The quote says only that these robots do not die or become inactive in a vacuum, with no remote operator.
A thumbprint on a door lock is fingerprint identification, but the 1965 NBS work targeted analysis of prints, not door locks.
A thinkwriter with a spool shows a tape in a writing machine only, with no sign of transcribing dictation.
Robot joints sending distress signals for lubrication is about internal self-monitoring, not a machine hearing.
A Speak-a-Type that rattles typing as she talks is speech converted to text; the dictated transcription matches Dragon Dictate, though keeping up is portrayed as clunky.
Walking inside a building-sized glass-fibre brain does not describe a neuron-style network that learns or recognizes.
Calculus machines that work out formulae are electronic computing, but code-breaking at Bletchley is a different function from general mathematics.
Worker machines modified for radio control by humans are operator-driven remote machines, though the goal is to stop revolt rather than handle hazards.
A metal-sinew humanoid body piloted from inside points loosely toward a humanoid robot, with no walking, speech or handling shown.
Making twenty-five chemical copies of a record describes duplication of a recording, not machine transcription.
Talking directly to a big computer and getting spoken answers is voice interaction, but how speech is produced is unspecified.
Rip plotting orbits for actual use hints at orbit calculation, but the quote lacks an onboard computer or maneuver.
Dialing the library and asking the robot for information matches remote retrieval, but nothing about stored collections or speed.
Burning out a calculator wing is physical destruction, a loose parallel to sabotage of computing.
A character stuffed with ragged bits of information has nothing to do with a 3D holographic display.
Thinking machines no bigger than a human brain match shrinking computing into tiny solid-state packages, but no technology is named.
A lock responding to a single chosen thought is thought-controlled machine access, though in reality an implant moves a cursor.
A cylinder seizing bodies and extracting minds is fantasy extraction, pointing loosely toward reading minds.
A chess machine analysing ten moves ahead is a computer chess program with a search depth, though the 1977 dedicated product was far weaker.
A burnished metal chart showing the heavens around the ship is a live position display of objects, similar in function to SAGE consoles.
A computer drawing an alien from recorded body specs is not about navigation or steering.
A robot that hears via an auditory mechanism like an electric eye is a machine sensing speech to respond, though crude.

A tone generator spanning audio range controlled rapidly by the machine in volume and pitch is electronic voice generation; Votrax-style synthesis matches, though 1959 context is a laboratory machine.
People living in machine-induced dreams with brains wired in point loosely at immersive worlds, not at headsets in arcades.
An audio-prompter telling children stories loosely suggests machine instruction, without lessons or grading.
A scanner that registers brain wave signature on a cylinder points loosely toward machine-held identity tokens, but no card is read.
A machine teaching grammar, vocabulary and arithmetic corresponds to computer-assisted instruction, though implanting directly differs.
Being registered on tape so alarms ring at the base boundary loosely suggests tracking people, with no worn transmitter.
Photos matched to an ident-card at police bureau use cards loosely, but nothing about a machine reading the card.
A ship computer that takes over, plots a course and picks a planet matches computer steering of a spacecraft, though autonomy is far beyond 1965.
Thought patterns detected and recorded for files loosely suggest reading brain signals, with no decoding of images.
Hurling an abstract concept into a machine to search a recording is thought-driven control of a device, but implanted-cursor control is far cruder.
Fixing sound receptors and a voice for a robot corresponds to machines hearing and speaking, but gives no generation mechanism.
Calling for every scrap of data on a planet from a central library is record retrieval on request, though film-based.
Putting a cylinder into an index system to learn everything about a person in minutes is retrieval of records, with the speed claim matching.
Robots querying the city library's automatic scanners is retrieval from a stored collection, with no detail on the search.
Going after something on the computer is only loosely computer-assisted investigation, with no record analysis.
A memory circuit that short-circuits against neural extraction is a biological defence, not about breaking into computers.
Robots with radio-senses tuned to those above show central direction of subordinate robots, but without a warehouse system.
A plan to build a dummy computer for fake results is about deception, not machine question answering.
The quote says no device detects telepathy, so it does not describe a machine reading specific thoughts.
A mansion that is completely automatic matches an automated house, though the quote offers no detail about occupants.
A mechanical brain assembling lists of prominent citizens by age on demand is machine retrieval of records from a store.
Winged silver robots commanding older ones show appearance only and no coordinated control.
The statement that the subject is an android is bare, and says nothing of an exact copy of a person.
Photographing retinas for the blood-vessel pattern matches scanning eye patterns to identify; the impersonation context differs from the 1981 commercial scanner.
Asking a character to elucidate has no machine navigation content.
A Brain controlling robots and a city with a mass limit matches central computing over robots, but without a fulfilment system.
Brain impulses turned into speech suggest a machine replying aloud, but ELIZA held typed conversation by pattern matching.
Creating a plane of artificial matter shows no control interface at all.
Punching coordinates into a large computer to guide a ship matches computer navigation, though mechanism is vague.
Figuring an interception orbit from sextant observations matches computed orbital manoeuvre, but not onboard in-flight.
A device converting computer tapes into patterns put into the brain is a computer-fed sensory world, but via neural stimulation rather than a display.
Huge punched-card files replacing slow human operators loosely suggest automated records, but not interactive search.
A seven-foot gleaming human-like robot matches a humanoid robot like Elektro, though only appearance is given.
A robot brain controlled telepathically through a throne transmitter is thought control by hidden transmitter, but the brain is not read.
An electronic analysis computer naming a murderer loosely echoes computerized crime records, but NCIC was just a database of wanted persons.
Brain impulses translated into sound broadcast through a speaker is speech generation, but with no synthesis method.
Ear-tubes that respond to sound as an input path match voice input to a computer, though recognition accuracy is not described.
Hypnotic rays implanting an experience loosely echo simulated worlds, but no computer-generated display.
A computer controlling all functions of a space station matches Skylab's computer, though Skylab's was limited to attitude and pointing.
Telepathic control of machines is vague about reading brain signals, so only loosely linked.
A robot pretending to be a man loosely points to a copy of a person, but no likeness is described.
A cap that reads thoughts and shows images on a screen is a thought display, but the milestone is text decoding from speech signals.
A lump behind the ear and a hidden tube describes an implant, but the cochlear implant restores hearing, which differs.
A central mechanical brain for national security loosely echoes SAGE computers, but SAGE guided air defence, not a general staff.
A navigator ignoring ribbing shows no navigation machine.
Robots making popular fiction is machine writing, but template forecasts are far from creative fiction.
Collecting thought as electric vibrations from the brain points toward reading brains, but without reconstructing a seen image.
A lock opening only to specified fingerprint patterns is fingerprint-based authentication, with matching detail absent.
A thumb in a whorl-lock opens a cabin door, a fingerprint recognition lock, mechanism unstated.
A giant computer with a Voder voice conversing fluently matches a talking conversation machine, but ELIZA only pattern-matched typed text.
A prosthetic device asked for limericks hints at conversation, but is very thin.
Recording a thumbprint to get aspirin from a machine is fingerprint identification for access, with no detail on matching.
Wristbands that sort people to levels loosely resemble machine-read tokens, but via vibrations rather than coded cards.
A Giant Brain you can ask questions of matches a question-answering computer, though conversational scope is only asserted.
Thoughts hurled at a computer's psychocoil is thought-based input, similar to a brain signal control, but with far greater ability.
A humandroid that looks and talks exactly like a named flyer is a copy of a particular person, a general match to Lincoln animatronics.
Calling a computer Mama magnified is about a maternal icon, not answering questions.
A machine that reads a mind and retranslates readings into images is a thought display, though the milestone decoded text instead.
A woman image synchronized to word impulses from a central computer is a face and voice front end, only loosely speech synthesis.
Eye and Brain coming later is a history of machine parts and not a sense of hearing.
A piano robot leading and giving rhythm to other robots is master robot coordinating subordinates, but in an orchestra setting.
Robots supervising robots are a hierarchy, loosely related to central coordination.
A lightweight no-back taken from a ship library suggests a portable reading device, but its form is unspecified.
A thumb on a doorplate with electronic grid is fingerprint reading, but the matching mechanism is only gestured at.
A chess machine seeing eight moves ahead matches game-tree chess play, but the quoted grandmaster claim far exceeds what was sold in 1977.
Machine-brain unbiased reasoning is a claim about rationality, not question answering.

A pineal analogue for extrasensory contact doesn't describe reading thoughts or images.
Dots in the tri-di tracking ships are a 3D track display, but the quote does not show holography.
Machine senses used for personality and smell are loosely artificial senses, but the milestone is a speech digit recognizer.
Faster chess machines outclassing humans is predicted, but the quote gives no program or play description.
Plotting a one-gee orbit by spoken order matches voice command to a machine, though recognition is not described.
Mechanical educators loosely echo teaching machines, but nothing of presenting lessons is stated.
A giant computer used to solve murders loosely echoes crime computing, but no records are described.

A transparent cube with full colour lights playing a recorded dream is a volumetric 3D display, though not a hologram.

Navigation charts with spark points for ships are a 3D position display, though not a holographic one.
